opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the big lesson for me was that you shouldn't start studying scaling laws too early. There's this temptation, especially if you've been around the big labs, to immediately start sweeping model sizes and data sizes and plotting nice log-log curves, because that's what serious people do. But when I was building the Go bot, I found that for a long time my curves were basically measuring bugs.

If your pipeline has some subtle issue, like your data augmentation is slightly off, or your value targets are noisy in a way you don't realize, or your self-play loop has some feedback problem, then you'll still get a curve. It might even look like a clean power law. But what you're really fitting is the scaling behavior of a broken system, and the exponents you extract don't mean much. You can end up making decisions about compute allocation based on an artifact.

So the heuristic I came away with is that you first need to get the thing to actually work at small scale, meaning it's learning what you think it's learning and you've hunted down the obvious failure modes. Only once the recipe is reasonably stable, where small changes in hyperparameters don't completely change the picture, is it worth investing in careful scaling studies. At that point they become really valuable, because they tell you whether to spend your next chunk of compute on a bigger network, more self-play games, or longer search.

Put another way, scaling laws are a tool for optimizing a recipe that already works, not for discovering whether you have one. For a solo project with limited compute, that ordering matters a lot, because every GPU hour spent on a premature sweep is one you didn't spend fixing the thing that was actually holding you back.

r001.rationale: The response says a broken pipeline can still produce a clean-looking power-law curve, including when data or the self-play loop has problems.

r002.rationale: It recommends first making the system work at small scale and stabilizing the recipe, then using scaling studies to guide compute allocation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the Go bot was a humbling little project. I built it back when AlphaGo had just come out, mostly because I wanted to understand what was actually going on under the hood rather than just read the paper. And the thing that stuck with me wasn't the algorithm, it was how badly my intuitions about compute were calibrated.

I'd write a policy network, train it for a few hours on a single GPU, and it would play like a mediocre amateur. And my instinct was always to go fiddle with the architecture or the search heuristics. Add a clever feature here, tweak the value head there. And those changes would give me these tiny bumps that felt like progress because I'd worked hard for them.

Then at some point I just let it train for a week with more self-play data, no changes to the model at all, and it blew past everything I'd done with cleverness. That was the moment I realized I'd been studying the wrong variable. I was treating compute and data as fixed constraints and trying to be smart within them, when the actual lever was the constraint itself.

So the lesson about scaling laws is that you should start studying them the moment you catch yourself being clever. If you've spent a week on a trick and you haven't asked what happens when you double the data or double the model, you're probably optimizing in the wrong dimension. The scaling curve is the baseline. Everything else has to beat the baseline, and most things don't.

The other thing it taught me is that small experiments are deceptive in a specific way. At small scale, the ranking of ideas is noisy and the cleverness looks like it matters a lot. As you scale up, a lot of that signal washes out and only the simple, general methods survive. So I'd say the time to start studying scaling laws is before you have the compute to need them, because you want to know which of your ideas will still be standing when you do.

astra-6.text: The lesson was to get something working before trying to understand how it scales. With the Go bot, there were so many basic things I could get wrong that a scaling study could easily have measured a bug or a bad design choice. Once you have a working system and can reliably improve it, studying scaling laws becomes useful: you can ask whether more compute or more data will keep paying off. Before that, I’d focus on getting the thing to learn at all.

sol-6.1.text: The lesson was that you should get something working before you start studying scaling laws. With the Go bot, I spent a lot of time thinking about how performance would scale with compute, but when your system is still small, a bug or a better design can matter much more than another order of magnitude of compute. First make sure it learns, make sure you can overfit a small problem, and understand what’s actually limiting it. Once you have a reasonably solid system and you’re deciding where to spend substantial compute, scaling laws become much more useful.
